analysis.one_liner: Bans gasoline exports whenever average US pump prices stay at or above $3.12 a gallon.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was introduced with no cosponsors in the final weeks of the 118th Congress and died in the House Foreign Affairs Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would order the President to ban exports of American gasoline whenever the national average price has been $3.12 per gallon or higher for seven straight days, with the ban lifting only after prices drop below that level for seven straight days. The idea is that keeping more gasoline at home during price spikes would add to domestic supply and help hold pump prices down. The President could grant exemptions and set the terms of the ban. It was introduced on the House floor on December 19, 2024, with no cosponsors, and referred to the Foreign Affairs Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and other gasoline consumers, who would benefit if more gasoline stayed in the domestic market during price spikes; a lower national average price even by a few cents saves households real money over a year.

how_it_helps.text: During any stretch when the national average gasoline price has been at or above $3.12 per gallon for seven consecutive days, the President must prohibit exporting US-produced gasoline, keeping that fuel in the domestic market [S2].

The ban stays in place until prices have been below $3.12 per gallon for seven consecutive days, so it automatically switches on and off with price conditions rather than requiring new legislation [S2].
The President can exempt exports deemed consistent with the national interest and set terms and conditions, giving the executive room to manage trade relationships while the ban is active [S2].

analysis.who_pays: US refiners and gasoline exporters, who would lose the ability to sell gasoline abroad whenever domestic prices cross the trigger level; foreign customers of US gasoline would also face reduced supply, which could invite retaliation or redirect trade.

drawbacks.text: The $3.12 trigger is a fixed number; if inflation or normal seasonal prices rise over time, the ban would switch on for long stretches at price levels that were once unremarkable, making an emergency measure into a near-permanent one [S2].

Economists generally argue crude oil prices are set in global markets, so blocking gasoline exports may not lower pump prices much; a refinery that loses export markets can cut output rather than flood the domestic market, and the threat of retaliation against other US exports is a real cost that supporters would have to weigh.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims directly at a cost households feel every week — pump prices — and its automatic trigger is a clean design. But the mechanism is unproven: gasoline is traded globally, prices are anchored to crude oil, and an export ban may deliver little relief while cutting refiners' revenues and exposing other US exports to retaliation. It also never got a hearing, so it was never tested against these objections.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last two weeks of the 118th Congress, sent to the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the Congress ended before it got a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the Gasoline Export Ban Act of 2024 on December 19, 2024 [S1].
On the day it was introduced, it was referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs [S4].
That referral was the bill's only action; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee without a hearing or vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US refiners and gasoline exporters are better off, since nothing restricts their ability to sell gasoline abroad during high-price periods. Drivers gained nothing, but the bill attracted no cosponsors, so its loss reflects the absence of support more than an organized defeat.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban gasoline exports during high-price periods

against.name: Michael McCaul
against.what_they_did: Committee took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was scheduled before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever held and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of potential support never formed.

industries.note: The bill would cut off a major sales channel whenever domestic pump prices crossed $3.12, directly reducing the revenue these companies earn selling US gasoline abroad. Their ability to keep that channel open runs against drivers' interest in lower pump prices.
Buyers abroad would lose access to US supply during high-price periods, and reduced availability could raise their costs; their loss is what the bill counts as a domestic gain.
